items.raw_snippet: 1) The “central bank” of the AI sector is in crisis. The chipmaker Nvidia has arguably been the single biggest beneficiary of the AI boom, with its market valuation rising by trillions of dollars since the release of ChatGPT. Partly for this reason, it has also functioned as the tech industry’s mini-Federal Reserve, acting as a funder and financial backstop for AI investment. [...] Nvidia’s falling valuation has left it with less spare cash for funding other AI ventures, and Huang’s departure has also reportedly sapped its interest in circular financing schemes. According to the Wall Street Journal, Nvidia’s new interim CEO, longtime finance chief Colette Kress, had privately pushed back against Huang’s increasingly ambitious investments in AI startups and data-center developers. At her behest, Nvidia halved a proposed $250 billion financial guarantee for an OpenAI [...] Nvidia did none of this out of charity. By facilitating the growth of AI labs and hyperscalers, the company increased demand for its own products. The aim was to foster a self-reinforcing cycle of spending: Nvidia puts money into AI companies, those companies buy its chips, the resulting revenue raises Nvidia’s valuation, which allows it to put more money into AI companies.

This paper studies how artificial intelligence (AI) affects the finance labor market when humans and AI perform different tasks in investment projects, and workers earn agency rents that grow with project size. We identify two key effects of AI improvement: A free-riding effect raises worker rents by increasing the probability of successful investment when the worker shirks; A capital reallocation effect shifts investment toward workers with higher or lower rents, depending on which tasks AI [...] on which tasks AI improves. The model generates predictions that would not obtain with a frictionless labor market. In particular, AI can increase labor demand and workers' rents even when substituting for workers. items.raw_snippet:
Artificial intelligence, or AI, is an umbrella term for software that performs tasks that would normally require human judgment. Think of recognizing patterns, sorting information or predicting what is likely to happen. In a business it's rarely anything spectacular. Most of the time it's a piece of software that makes an existing work process faster or more accurate.

The applications we see most often in practice are: [...] In a business you mainly come across applications such as document processing, classification, forecasting, anomaly detection and intelligent routing. So it's about what the software does, not an abstract label. Choose the type that fits your problem.

### What does AI stand for?

AI stands for artificial intelligence, or kunstmatige intelligentie in Dutch. In Dutch texts you'll see both terms used interchangeably, and they mean the same thing. [...] AI is the broad term for software that performs tasks that would normally require human judgment. ChatGPT is one specific application of it, focused on language and conversation. For many business processes, such as reading documents or flagging deviations, you need something other than a chat window.

In this edition of “Ask the Board,” we feature Lisa Nichols, Co-founder and CEO of Technology Partners, a technology consulting, staffing, and AI solutions firm she has led for more than 30 years with her husband, Greg. [...] No one has AI completely figured out. That's OK. Companies should be creating a culture where people can experiment, share ideas, and learn from one another. Encourage employees to demonstrate new AI tools they've discovered, talk about what's working, and be honest about what isn't. Curiosity is one of the best investments any business can make.

## Measure success by what AI allows your people to do [...] AI can help summarize meetings, organize information, and automate routine tasks. That gives people more time to do the work technology can't replace. Communication, creativity, judgment, empathy, relationship-building, and leadership are becoming even more valuable in an AI-enabled workplace. Continue investing in those skills just as intentionally as you invest in new technology.
